Countries like Germany and Sweden have seen over 20% growth in their Muslim communities since 2010, largely due to both legal immigration and high birth rates. This influx far exceeds that of other immigrant groups, suggesting a pattern rather than random migration. Critics of the Great Replacement theory attribute this to economic and refugee crises, yet proponents highlight the rapidity and scale of these changes, which align with ideological goals of cultural expansion.

Muslims in Western countries often exhibit birth rates significantly above the replacement level (2.1 children per woman). Counterarguments and Rebuttals

Birth rate disparities may reflect socioeconomic factors, but elevated fertility among Muslim communities remains statistically significant.     • Terror attacks, grooming scandals, or high-profile controversies around religion can make “Islam” feel more omnipresent than it is statistically.

  4. Distrust in institutions
